title: Broken Order
focus: Binary search when the sort is rotated, prefix sums that update, and the DP that runs on intervals.

cards.title: Rotated Sorted Search
cards.trigger: A sorted array that has been rotated, and you still want O(log n).
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the claim the whole solution rests on: for any mid, at least one of the two halves is fully sorted. Why is that always true?
useWhen: Search in a rotated sorted array
Find the minimum in a rotated sorted array
Find how many times the array was rotated
Peak element in a bitonic array
Any array with one break in monotonicity
template: if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:              # LEFT half is sorted
if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]:  lo, hi = lo, mid - 1
if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]:  lo, hi = mid + 1, hi
# Minimum in a rotated array: compare mid against hi, never against lo
if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1     # minimum is strictly right
else:                    hi = mid         # mid could be the minimum
keyInsights: The rotation point sits in exactly one half, so the other half is unbroken. Identify the sorted half, then a plain range test decides
For the minimum, compare mid against hi. Comparing against lo is ambiguous when the array is not rotated at all
`nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` uses `<=` so a two-element window still classifies correctly
cards.trap: 'Duplicates are allowed.' `nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi]` tells you nothing, you shrink by one, and the worst case degrades to O(n). Say that out loud, it is the expected answer.

cards.title: Fenwick Tree (BIT)
cards.trigger: Prefix or range queries on an array that keeps changing.
cards.recall: Write both loops from memory. Then answer what makes it work: what does `i & -i` compute, and what range of the original array does index i of the tree cover?
useWhen: Range sum with point updates
Count of smaller numbers after self, after coordinate compression
Count inversions in an array
Running rank or order statistics
Any prefix aggregate under updates, when a segment tree is more than you need
template: def update(self, i, delta):         # i is 1-based
i += i & -i                 # jump to the next covering node
def query(self, i):                 # prefix sum of [1, i]
i -= i & -i                 # strip the lowest set bit
# Count smaller after self: iterate right to left, query then update

problem.name: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

keyInsights: `i & -i` isolates the lowest set bit, which is exactly the length of the range that node covers
1-indexed is not a preference. `i & -i` is zero at index 0 and the loop never advances
A merge sort with a counting step solves the same problems in O(n log n) without any bit tricks. Offer both
cards.trap: 'Now support range updates as well as range queries.' You need two BITs and a small algebraic derivation. Know that it exists rather than inventing it live.

cards.title: Restructure In Place
cards.trigger: Turn a tree into a different shape without allocating new nodes.
cards.recall: Write the flatten from memory using the predecessor method. Then answer why processing in reverse preorder, right then left then node, makes the naive version work in O(1) space.
useWhen: Flatten a binary tree to a linked list
Convert a BST to a sorted doubly linked list
Increasing order search tree
Populate next right pointers
Any in-place structural rewiring
template: # O(1) space: for each node, splice the left subtree into the right chain
while pred.right:           # rightmost node of the left subtree
pred.right = node.right     # it inherits the current right chain
node.right = node.left      # left subtree becomes the right chain
# O(h) alternative: reverse preorder with a running 'previous'

problem.name: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List

keyInsights: The rightmost node of the left subtree is the last node of the left chain, so it is exactly where the old right chain reattaches
Reverse preorder means every node is rewired only after everything that follows it is already a chain
Setting `node.left = None` is mandatory. Leaving it produces a structure that prints correctly and is still wrong
cards.trap: 'Do it as a doubly linked list, circular, from a BST.' Same idea, inorder instead of preorder, plus stitching the head to the tail at the end.

cards.title: Interval DP
cards.trigger: The state is a range of the input, and it is built from strictly shorter ranges.
cards.recall: Write longest palindromic subsequence from memory. Then answer the loop-order question: why must `i` descend, or equivalently why fill by increasing interval length?
useWhen: Longest palindromic subsequence
Minimum insertions or deletions to make a palindrome
Matrix chain multiplication, burst balloons, stone games
Optimal binary search tree
Any DP where the state is a subarray or substring
template: # dp[i][j] = longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j]
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):        # i DESCENDING
for j in range(i + 1, n):          # j ascending
# Minimum insertions to make a palindrome = n - lps(s)
keyInsights: dp[i][j] reads dp[i+1][j-1], a strictly shorter interval, so shorter intervals must already be filled. That is the loop order
LPS of s equals LCS of s and its reverse. If you know one you know the other
The answer lives at dp[0][n-1], not at dp[n][n]. Interval DP answers sit in a corner, not on the diagonal
cards.trap: 'Burst balloons.' Same table, but the recurrence loops over which balloon is burst LAST, not first. That inversion is what makes the subproblems independent.

cards.title: Grid Backtracking
cards.trigger: Find a path through a grid spelling something, where cells cannot be reused within a path.
cards.recall: Write word search from memory. Then answer the difference that matters: in flood fill you never unmark, here you must. Why?
useWhen: Word search on a board
Word search II, many words, add a trie
Unique paths III, visit every open cell exactly once
Rat in a maze, all paths from corner to corner
Any grid path where the visited set is per-path, not global
template: if r < 0 or r >= rows or c < 0 or c >= cols: return False
board[r][c] = '#'                       # mark for THIS path only
found = (go(r+1, c, i+1) or go(r-1, c, i+1) or
go(r, c+1, i+1) or go(r, c-1, i+1))
board[r][c] = word[i]                   # unmark on the way out
return any(go(r, c, 0) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols))
keyInsights: Flood fill asks 'is this cell in any region', so a global mark is correct. Path search asks 'is this cell on this path', so the mark must be undone
Restoring the original character rather than a placeholder means no extra storage at all
Checking the character before marking prunes three quarters of the branches for free
cards.trap: 'Now search a hundred words on the same board.' One DFS per word times out. Build a trie of all words and walk board and trie together, deleting words as you find them.
